query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In corrosion‐resistant high‐Cr steels, the enhanced performance in chemical-processing and nuclear-power environments is achieved by the in situ formation of a continuous, nanocrystalline chromium-rich oxide layer that is stabilized by chromium segregation at grain boundaries. This passive film acts as an effective barrier to the ingress of corrosive species.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-Cr stainless steel with a uniform microstructure and controlled grain size distribution, wherein chromium is homogeneously distributed prior to any oxidative treatment.
generation.intervention: A controlled oxidation or annealing treatment under a defined oxygen potential to initiate passive film formation, followed by exposure to a corrosive environment (e.g., an acidic chloride solution or high-temperature water) that simulates chemical-processing and nuclear conditions (optionally with low-level ion irradiation to mimic nuclear effects).
generation.conditions: Temperature ranging from ambient to about 300°C typical of processing environments, with controlled oxygen partial pressure. In the nuclear context, exposure may include a simulated irradiation flux at moderate dose rates; corrosive electrolyte concentrations should be moderate enough to allow passivation mechanisms to be observed.
generation.structural_mediator: A nanocrystalline chromium-rich oxide layer (the passive film) along with chromium segregation at grain boundaries, which together enhance the barrier properties against corrosive species.
generation.mechanism: Upon exposure to an oxidizing environment, chromium atoms diffuse from the bulk and segregate to grain boundaries and the surface, where they preferentially oxidize to form a tightly adherent, nanostructured Cr-rich oxide film. This film minimizes the diffusion of aggressive ions (such as chloride) into the substrate. Under simulated irradiation conditions, the fine-grained microstructure is hypothesized to promote rapid self-repair of any damaged film areas through increased Cr diffusion, thereby maintaining passivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to steels without an optimized Cr content or controlled grain structure, treated steels will exhibit significantly lower corrosion rates (e.g., reduced corrosion current densities and higher pitting potentials) when exposed to corrosive media. Microscopic analysis (e.g., TEM/EDS) will reveal a uniform, nano-scale Cr-rich passive layer in the treated samples versus a disrupted or thinner oxide layer in untreated controls.
generation.baseline: Steels with lower Cr content or with a microstructure that discourages Cr segregation (e.g., coarse grains or after pre-treatment that depletes surface Cr) will form either discontinuous or less protective oxide films, exhibiting higher corrosion rates (more pitting and uniform corrosion) under the same environmental conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for steels with a chromium content above a threshold (typically above 12-15 wt%) and for environments where an oxidizing condition is present at moderate temperatures and corrosive ion concentrations. Under extremely aggressive conditions (e.g., very high chloride concentrations) or for steels with alternative alloying compositions that significantly modify diffusional behavior, the mechanism may not fully apply.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative role of Cr segregation and passive film formation is well established, the exact effect of nanostructuring and the quantitative thresholds (in terms of Cr content and grain size) under simultaneous irradiation remain to be precisely determined. The effect of irradiation on film stability is also not fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of steel samples varying in Cr content and grain size. Subject a subset to a controlled oxidation/annealing treatment designed to promote passive film formation. Expose both treated and untreated samples to a corrosive environment (e.g., acidic chloride solution at elevated temperature) with and without a simulated low-level irradiation source to mimic nuclear conditions. Use microscopic and electrochemical analysis to assess film formation and corrosion behavior.
measurements: Characterization of the oxide film thickness, nano-structure, and composition via TEM/EDS or XPS
Corrosion current density and pitting potential from potentiodynamic polarization tests
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to assess barrier properties
Pre- and post-exposure microstructural evaluation of grain boundary Cr segregation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high-Cr steels with controlled grain structures do not exhibit the formation of a continuous, nanocrystalline Cr-rich oxide layer or if their corrosion rates are not significantly lower than those of the control samples (with disrupted or absent passive films) under both non-irradiated and simulated irradiation conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.
